question: An engineering lead is reviewing a colleague's caching design for a document Q&A tool. The design places cache_control on the final message of each request, where the final message is the user's newest question, which is different on every request. Static content such as the system prompt and the large source document appears earlier in the request and is never marked with cache_control. What is the most likely outcome of this design?
options: A) The design is optimal, because placing cache_control on the most recent content guarantees the freshest possible cache entry for every request

B) The design will still cache the static system prompt and document automatically, because cache_control breakpoints apply retroactively to all earlier stable content regardless of where they are placed

C) Little to no cache benefit will be realized, because the breakpoint is placed on content that changes every request, so the cache is effectively rewritten from scratch each time rather than being reused
D) The design will cause an API error, because cache_control cannot be applied to the final block in a request under any circumstances
correct_answers: C) Little to no cache benefit will be realized, because the breakpoint is placed on content that changes every request, so the cache is effectively rewritten from scratch each time rather than being reused
explanations: "Freshest content" is not what caching optimizes for; caching benefits come from reusing a stable prefix across requests, and marking constantly changing content defeats that goal rather than achieving it.

Caching is not retroactive or automatic based on stability; the breakpoint marks where the cache is written, and only content up to and including that breakpoint's position is cached, so placing it on the wrong block leaves the earlier static content uncached.

Correct. Best practice is to place cache_control on stable content so subsequent requests can match the cached prefix; here the breakpoint sits on the ever-changing final user question, so the prefix hash differs every request, preventing reuse of the cache for the static system prompt and document.

There is no restriction against applying cache_control to a final block generally; the problem here is a design/effectiveness issue (marking changing content), not an API-level restriction causing an error.
